AN ACT to amend the public health law, in relation to establishing the primary
care reform commission
items.lawCode: Amd Art 29-AA Art Head, add §2959-b, Pub Health L
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S6534

SPONSOR: RIVERA
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public health law, in relation to establishing the
primary care reform commission

 
PURPOSE:

This bill establishes the primary care reform commission to review the
level of primary care spending in the state and make recommendations for
how to increase the level of high-quality primary care and primary care
spending.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 adds a new article heading to article 29-aa of the public
health law, as added by section 35 of part H of chapter 59 of the laws
of 2011, to read: Patient Centered Medical Homes and Primary Care.

Section 2 amends the public health law by adding a new section 2959-b
which establishes the primary care reform commission. This section
provides for the responsibilities of the commission, which is to review
and make findings on the level of primary care spending by all payments,
in the context of overall healthcare spending in the state.  Members
shall be appointed by the governor with recommendations from the Legis-
lature and are to have qualifications which include expertise in health-
care financing, reimbursement, and regulation within the categories of
primary care providers and administrators from health centers or profes-
sional practice groups, state operating businesses, public and commer-
cial health insurance plans, primary care professionals, and advocacy
organizations. The commission is to publish and deliver an annual report
to the governor and the Legislature to include an analysis of current
primary care spending, recommendations on the definition of "primary
care", recommendations for new legislation, identification of barriers
to providing primary care, recommendations to improve providing higher-
quality primary care and primary care spending and recommendations to
increase primary care spending to be the greater of 12 % or a 1%
increase each year of overall healthcare spending of 2026, among other
provisions.

Each Medicaid managed care provider or Insurance entity that provides
managed care products, individual comprehensive accident and health
insurance, a group of blanket comprehensive health and accident insur-
ance, or plan in which the department of financial services has juris-
diction, are to provide primary care spending data. This data is to
include primary care spending, total healthcare spending, and any
further information requested by the commission. There is to be estab-
lished requirements that ensure compliance and privacy of information.

Provides for definitions of "primary care", "primary care spending", and
"Medicaid managed care provider."

Section 3 provides for the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:


Primary care is underfunded and underutilized, despite a robust body of
evidence that it is critical to overall health and wellness and is a
driving factor in reducing health care costs. It is estimated that as
little as 5-7% of U.S. health care spending goes to primary care, which
has detrimental downstream effects on community health and health care
costs. New York State spends about 20% more than the national average in
per person health care costs, but consistently ranks below other states
in key health indicators such as preventable hospitalizations, birth
weight, and childhood immunizations, among others.

Lack of investment in primary care and prevention has led to rising
health care costs and rates of chronic illnesses, leaving New Yorkers
vulnerable to threats like COVID-19. Many neighborhoods across the State
with high rates of COVID-19 infection and poor primary care access are
low-income and predominantly people of color, who experience high rates
of chronic disease. Increased access to primary care is the first line
of defense for these communities in the face of the ongoing COVID-19
pandemic as well as future disease threats.  Research shows that an
increase of just one primary care provider per 10,000 people can lead to
5.5% fewer hospital visits, 11% fewer emergency department visits, and
7% fewer surgeries.

To date, at least ten states have acted to rebalance - rather than
increase their health care spending to strengthen primary care through
legislative, regulatory, or executive means. New York State must be
next. New York's underserved communities have a pressing need for prima-
ry care, yet the providers and institutions that serve them have been
unable to sufficiently sustain, expand, and improve services due to
systemic underfunding and undervaluing of primary care services. To that
end, this legislation creates a commission charged with defining, meas-
uring, and reporting on current primary care expenditures, and making
recommendations on how to increase the proportion of health care funding
that goes to primary care across all payers in New York. To improve the
health of all communities across the State, New York must ensure that
the provision of primary care services is prioritized and funded. This
bill institutes a long-term approach to ensuring all New Yorkers have
access to primary care services.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

A.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S6534A

SPONSOR: RIVERA
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public health law, in relation to establishing the
primary care reform commission

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

Stakeholders would develop recommendations as to how much and by what
means the proportion of health care spending that goes to primary care
services should increase.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

A new section 2959-b is added to the Public Health law. The Primary care
refoini commission is constituted and charged. Participants would
include experts on health care financing, reimbursement, and regulation
from primary care providers, federally qualified health centers and
professional practice groups, as well as representatives with relevant
expertise from businesses operating within New York, public and commer-
cial health plans including managed care plans, and primary care profes-
sional and advocacy organizations. Third party payors would be compelled
to provide data requested by the commission, with protections for
proprietary property. The first report of recommendations would be
published by March 31, 2022, including a comparative analysis of current
primary care spending, and recommendations to the Governor and the
legislature regarding the barriers to primary care and how to overcome
them.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Primary care should be person's first contact with the health care
system. Primary care is understanding and maintaining wellness, and
identifying and treating illness before it becomes a chronic condition.
Research shows that an increase of just one primary care provider per
10,000 people can generate 5.5% fewer hospital visits, 11% fewer emer-
gency department visits, and 7% fewer surgeries. We know that health
systems oriented towards primary care simply function better. Yet, it is
estimated that as little as 5% of U.S.  health care spending goes toward
primary care. New York currently spends more per capita on health care
than the national average, but consistently ranks below many other
states in key health indicators.  This is indicative of a lack of access
to and an underinvestment in primary care.

Currently, at least ten states have acted to rebalance their health care
spending through legislative, regulatory, or executive means.  This
commission will define, measure, and report on current primary care
spending in New York. Further, the commission will identify the means to
increase the proportion of the health care dollar that goes to primary
care services across all payers, for the benefit of all patients. An
ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:
None.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
Immediately.
